# Ecclesiastes Chapter 7 -- The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

**1** A good reputation is more valuable than expensive perfume; the day you die is better than the day you are born.

**2** Better to spend your time at funerals than at parties. After all, everyone dies — so the living should take this to heart.

**3** Sorrow is better than laughter, for sadness has a refining influence on us.

**4** A wise person thinks a lot about death, while a fool thinks only about having a good time.

**5** Better to be criticized by a wise person than to be praised by a fool.

**6** A fool's laughter is like thorns crackling under a pot — loud and useless. This too is fleeting.

**7** Extortion turns a wise person into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart.

**8** Finishing is better than starting, and patience is better than pride.

**9** Control your temper, for anger makes its home in the heart of fools.

**10** Don't long for "the good old days." This is not wise thinking.

**11** Wisdom is even better when you have money. Both are a benefit as you go through life.

**12** Wisdom and money can both get you through, but the advantage of wisdom is that it preserves your life.

**13** Accept the way God does things, for who can straighten what he has made crooked?

**14** Enjoy prosperity while you can, but when hard times strike, realize that both come from God. Remember that nothing is certain in this life.

**15** I have seen everything during my fleeting life — including the righteous person who dies young and the wicked person who lives to a ripe old age.

**16** So don't be too good or too wise! Why destroy yourself? **17** On the other hand, don't be too wicked either. Don't be a fool! Why die before your time?

**18** Pay attention to both of these warnings. If you fear God, you will succeed in either case.

**19** One wise person is stronger than ten city officials.

**20** Not a single person on earth is always good and never sins.

**21** Don't eavesdrop on others — you might hear your servant cursing you. **22** For you know in your heart that you have cursed others many times.

**23** I said to myself, "I am determined to be wise." But it didn't work. **24** Wisdom is always just out of reach. It is deep, deep beyond discovery.

**25** I searched everywhere, determined to find wisdom and to understand the reason for things. I also wanted to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the madness of foolishness.

**26** I discovered that a seductive woman is a trap more bitter than death. Her heart is a snare, and her hands are chains. A person who pleases God will escape her, but she will catch the sinner.

**27** "This is my conclusion," says the Teacher. "I discovered this after looking at the matter from every angle. **28** Though I have searched repeatedly, I have not found what I was looking for. Only one man in a thousand is virtuous, but not one woman. **29** But I did find this: God created people to be virtuous, but they have each turned to follow their own downward path."

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The counter-intuitive openings (vv.1-6):** Qoheleth opens with a series of shocking "better...than" statements that reverse conventional wisdom. Death is better than birth; mourning is better than feasting; sorrow is better than laughter. The point is not pessimism but depth — encounters with mortality and suffering produce wisdom that comfort and pleasure cannot.

**Don't be too righteous (v.16):** This is one of Ecclesiastes' most misunderstood passages. Qoheleth is not advising moral mediocrity. He's warning against a self-righteous rigidity that, in trying to control every outcome through moral perfection, ends up destroying the person who practices it. The parallel warning against excessive wickedness (v.17) shows this is about pragmatic realism, not moral indifference.

**The "woman" passage (vv.26-28):** These verses have a long history of misogynistic interpretation. In the ancient Near Eastern wisdom tradition, the "dangerous woman" was a stock figure representing not all women but a specific threat to the young man's formation. Some scholars read this as allegory: Wisdom herself (personified as female in Proverbs 1-9) is elusive and entangling. The verse count — one man in a thousand, no woman — may express Qoheleth's broader point that uprightness is nearly impossible for anyone.

*-- PNEUMA*
